HFGCS · Group 4 long messages · 248 distinct messages of 54+ characters · Jan 2022 – Sep 2026

Long-EAM Block Grammar

The long Group 4 messages are built from fields, and every field is closed by a marker. Read that way, 166 of the 248 parse into marker-closed rows with nothing left over — a two-part head, a run of 22-character blocks, a 9-character trailer, and a small set of optional parts — and 15 more do the same apart from row A, whose echo went missing for a stretch of 2023 and 2024. Their lengths come out of one formula; what falls outside it has its own sections below.

Three markers, one rule

Quad
GGGG

Four identical characters. Closes the B field and every body block; sits at the slot. 77% of all slots. A triple with one more character (LLL2) does the same job in one message.

Echo X??X
K7BK

First and fourth character equal. Closes the A field (positions 21–24) and the A′ field of an extra head. At a slot with no quad it sits five before the slot (13 + 4) — or, rarely, one past it (18 + 4), or in the slot itself as it does in row A.

Double ##
TT

Two identical characters, not part of a longer run. Closes the short fields of the ##-runs, the 3 + ## stub, and most of the 108's fields. In 7 messages it also stands in for the quad, filling the first two characters of every marker slot while the last two run on as text; and in 9 it closes row A in place of the echo, in the field's last two characters (9 against 1.3 expected).

A row is a field plus its marker, and rows break only at markers; the trailer is the last nine characters. Every card below is rendered from that rule alone — markers are computed, never hand-placed — and the copy dot before a message puts its full string on the clipboard.

quad echo at a boundary incidental X??X (base rate, left visible) ## double extra head (A′ · B′) prefix left number = row start · then the row's length and what closes it

One formula

A message is a prefix, a row A, a trailer, and a choice of parts between them. Which parts, and how many, fix the length.

L  =  PR + A + B + n·blk + k·(A′ + B′) + [ext] + [A′ + run] + T

      n  body blocks, 0 or more          k  extra heads, 0, 1 or 2          [ ]  optional

      with neither option        L  =  54 + 22n + 38k
      the short forms            L  =  33 + run          PR + A + run + T
TermSizeWhat it is
PR2the two-letter prefix
A18 + 4 = 22the first head field, closed by an echo X??X at 21–24
B17 + 4 = 21the second head field, closed by the first quad
blk18 + 4 = 22a body block, closed by a quad — or by a triple, or by a doubled pair at the slot's start; or, at a slot with no marker at all, by an echo five before it (13 + 4, then the B shape follows) or one after it (18 + 4)
A′ · B′17 · 21an extra head: an A-shaped field five shorter, then a B-shaped field. Seen on the grid as a 16-character insert; 34 messages carry one, 2 carry two
extn36 · 40 · 46 · 52a longer field in front of a B-shaped row, closed by an echo — 32, 36, 42 or 48 characters plus its marker. In front of B′ it can appear as a run of 23 followed by a 13 + 4 field instead. 29 messages
run23232 + X??X, then 3 + ##, 4 + ##, 4 + ##. The opening echo is there in 12 of the 14 — it is what makes this run a different object from the 29. Carried by the 56, 94, 108, 172, 198, 222 and 286
run29299 + ##, 6 + ##, 2 + ##, 4 + ## — no opening echo in any of the 15. Carried by the 62, 102, 166, 188 and 210
stub5the final block in echo-closed form — same 22 characters, so the length does not move. 14 messages
3535after an A′, 35 characters with no closer at all, in place of the last two blocks — the 172, 194 and 216. 15 messages
T9the last nine characters. Not quite unmarked: a gap-4 echo spanning its 4th and 8th characters turns up in 25 of the 248 messages against 8 expected. One family, the 68, closes on 8 instead (10 messages)

Read it as an inventory, not a template. It counts the parts and always sums to the length, but it does not fix their order: in 19 messages the blocks come after the extra head — PR + A + B + 3 blk + A′ + B′ + 4 blk + T is the 286 — and in the 210 the run comes before them. Two things sit outside it: A′ + 35, a tail with no closer at all (the 172, 194 and 216), and the 108 and 176, which have no blocks at all and are written in their own field sizes. The census at the end is in these terms, taken from each message's own rows, so it shows the order the message used — and every line of it sums to its length.

The runs 31 messages across 12 lengths

Two of the parts are runs of short ##-closed fields, and they are not the same object. run23 opens with a 2 + X??X field — present in 12 of its 14 appearances — and continues 3 + ##, 4 + ##, 4 + ##. run29 opens with 9 + ## and continues 6 + ##, 2 + ##, 4 + ##, and never carries that opening echo in any of its 15. Where a run sits is what changes with length: in the 56 and the 62 it is the whole body, PR + A + run + T; after an A′ it is the tail that replaces the last two blocks; in front of a B-shaped row it does the work of an extension. So the short forms and the long ones are the same construction with different amounts in front of the run — 166 − 62 = 104 = B + 3 blk + A′, and 94 − 56 = 38 = B + A′.

The 56 and the 62 are one family in every respect but which run they use: they share three of their nineteen days (0.41 expected, p = 0.005), and both were closer-free until 240609 and closed ever after — the first closed 56 and the first closed 62 went out under the same prefix 59 minutes apart. The 108 belongs here too: four of its five messages carry the run23 entire, at 25–47, before going on to fields the block grammar does not use.

Lineage within a prefix reign 135 message pairs · 135 same-prefix · 0 cross-prefix

Flip up and down through the decks above and the cards look like variants of one another. They are: long messages under one prefix are partial copies of earlier ones. Seeding on shared six-character runs and scoring every offset, 135 pairs share far more identical characters at one constant offset than chance allows (z ≥ 15; same-day re-reads excluded) — and all of them are the same prefix. An exhaustive scan of all 36,315 pairs, which also catches copies with no six-character run in common, raises that to 169, still every one of them same-prefix; none crosses a prefix change. What is kept follows the block: positions 1–4, 10–12 and 18–22, which carry the marker, are kept about 64% of the time, while two five-character windows, 5–9 and 13–17, are re-keyed (17% identical). Row A is never copied; the trailer is. A long message is a frame with two payload windows per block.

Two lengths of short fields the 108 · the 176

Two lengths have no blocks at all and are written entirely in short ##-closed fields. The 108 opens with the run23, as above, and then goes on with seven closers of its own, in the same places in four of its five messages. The 176 has twelve closers running at a spacing of six in three groups, the groups 40 apart. A run of three or more ## at spacing six occurs in no other message in the corpus, and in none of 300 shuffles of these two. Their rows are right-aligned so the closers line up.

What is left over 35 messages the rules do not reach

62 messages carry no quad anywhere, so they have no grid of block markers at all. 27 of them still read: the run-carrying short forms, the 108 and the 176, and the 68, which puts one long echo-closed field between A and the trailer and ends on eight rather than nine. The other 35 are the bulk of what this page cannot read — though most still open the same way, with a closer at position 24 where row A ends, in 15 of the 19 longest. Within a length the evidence for anything further is thin: a shared closer or two, holding on two or three members.
